sections.title: How Are Electrons Distributed in Different Energy Levels?
Combining Capacity of an Atom: Valency

slides.title: Bohr and Bury Shell Rules
slides.kicker: Electrons live in shells, not in chaos
bullets: Bohr and Bury suggested rules for how many electrons each shell of an atom can hold.
The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by the formula 2n^2, where n is the shell number.
Shells are filled stepwise, starting from the one closest to the nucleus and moving outward.
slides.note: 2n^2 is the seating plan of every shell — yaad rakhna!

slides.title: The 2n^2 Formula at Work
slides.kicker: One formula, every shell's capacity
bullets: K-shell: n = 1, so 2 x 1^2 = 2 electrons.
L-shell: n = 2, so 2 x 2^2 = 8 electrons.
M-shell: n = 3, so 2 x 3^2 = 18 electrons.

slides.title: Outermost Shell Cap: Eight
slides.kicker: The outside seat limit is eight
bullets: The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the outermost shell is 8.
The first shell is the exception: it can accommodate a maximum of 2 electrons.
So the M-shell, though able to hold 18, stops at 8 when it is the outermost shell.

slides.title: Filling Order: K to N
slides.kicker: Front benches first, then back rows
bullets: Electrons are filled in the shells in a stepwise manner, starting from the one closest to the nucleus.
The order of filling is K, L, M, N and onward.
The L-shell is filled only after the K-shell is complete, and so on.
slides.note: No jumping the queue — shells fill in order!

slides.title: First Atoms: H and He
slides.kicker: Hydrogen one seat, helium two seats
bullets: Hydrogen has atomic number 1, so its only electron has to be in the K-shell.
Helium contains two protons in its nucleus and two electrons.
Both helium electrons fit into the K-shell, which holds a maximum of 2.

items: Its single electron goes into the K-shell
Helium: two protons and two electrons
Both electrons sit in the K-shell

slides.title: Building Atoms Step by Step
slides.kicker: Add one electron, bump the count
bullets: We can create two-dimensional atomic structures for various elements.
Add one electron to the appropriate energy level each time the atomic number is increased by 1.
Repeating this builds up the atomic structures of the elements, one electron at a time.

items: Add one electron to the right shell
Repeat and watch the atom grow

slides.title: What Is Electronic Configuration?
slides.kicker: The shell-wise address of electrons
bullets: The distribution of electrons among various shells is known as the electronic configuration of the atom.
Table 8.4 lists symbols, atomic numbers, protons, neutrons, electrons and shell-wise electron distribution for the first eighteen elements.
Fig. 8.11 shows schematic atomic structures of the first eighteen elements with electrons in the K, L and M shells.

slides.title: Riddle: The Soft Metal
slides.kicker: Mass 23, protons 11 — who am I?
bullets: A riddle from the book: I am an atom with a mass number of 23 and 11 protons.
I am a soft metal and I react vigorously with water.
Neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12, so I have 12 neutrons. I am sodium!

items: Protons given: 11, so atomic number is 11
Atomic number 11 means the element is sodium

slides.note: The book dares you to build your own riddle — try one!

slides.title: Combining Capacity Basics
slides.kicker: Count the hydrogens an atom joins
bullets: Combining capacity is the number of hydrogen or chlorine atoms with which one atom of an element can combine.
It is expressed using hydrogen and chlorine because both have a combining capacity of one.
In H2O (water), oxygen combines with two hydrogen atoms, so the combining capacity of oxygen is two.

slides.title: Valence Shell and Electrons
slides.kicker: The outermost ring does the talking
bullets: The outermost shell containing electrons of an atom is known as its valence shell.
The electrons present in the valence shell are known as valence electrons.
The combining capacity of an atom is decided by its electronic configuration, so valence electrons matter most.

slides.title: Octet: The Stability Rule
slides.kicker: Eight outside means calm and stable
bullets: If the outermost shell of an atom has 8 electrons, it is called an octet.
Elements with a complete octet, or 2 electrons for helium, are largely unreactive and more stable.
Atoms with incomplete valence shells are usually more reactive; they lose, gain, or share electrons to complete their octet.

slides.title: Finding Valency: Three Cases
slides.kicker: Lose, gain or share to reach eight
bullets: Valency is the number of electrons gained, lost, or shared to complete the octet.
Fewer than four valence electrons: the element tends to lose them. Sodium, 2, 8, 1, loses one, so its valency is 1.
More than four: it tends to gain. Oxygen, 2, 6, gains two, so its valency is 2.
slides.note: Carbon, 2, 4, can do neither easily, so it shares all four — valency 4!

slides.title: Twin Atoms: Isotopes
slides.kicker: Same protons, different neutrons
bullets: Dalton proposed that all atoms of an element are identical and have the same mass.
Scientists later found atoms of the same element with the same atomic number Z but different numbers of neutrons.
These 'twin atoms' with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (A = protons + neutrons) are called isotopes.

slides.title: Hydrogen's Three Isotopes
slides.kicker: One proton each, zero to two neutrons
bullets: Naturally occurring hydrogen is a mixture of three isotopes: protium, deuterium and tritium.
Protium is about 99.98 percent, deuterium about 0.015 percent, and tritium occurs only in traces.
All three contain one proton each, while deuterium has one neutron and tritium has two.

slides.title: Same Chemistry, Different Physics
slides.kicker: Electrons decide chemistry, not neutrons
bullets: The chemical properties of isotopes are similar because they have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration.
Chemical properties depend mainly on the number of valence electrons.
Isotopes differ in their physical properties, for example boiling and melting points.

slides.title: Carbon Isotopes, Tiny Units
slides.kicker: Weighing atoms needs a microscale
bullets: Carbon has three isotopes, C-12, C-13 and C-14; each has six protons and six electrons.
They differ only in the number of neutrons, and C-12 is the most abundant isotope in nature.
Atomic masses are measured in the unified atomic mass unit (u) because a kilogram is too large for atoms; earlier it was called amu.
slides.note: Like weighing a grain of wheat in milligrams, not kilograms — the book's own comparison!

slides.title: Isotopes at Work in Life
slides.kicker: From power plants to ancient fossils
bullets: U-235, an isotope of uranium, is used as a fuel in nuclear reactors to generate electricity in nuclear power plants.
Co-60, a radioactive isotope of cobalt, is used in radiation treatment for cancer.
I-131 treats goitre and thyroid cancer, and C-14 helps archaeology and geology date ancient fossils and artefacts.

slides.title: Isobars: Same Mass Number
slides.kicker: Different elements, equal nucleon total
bullets: Calcium (atomic number 20), potassium (atomic number 19) and argon (atomic number 18) each have a mass number of 40.
They have different numbers of protons, yet the total number of nucleons in their atoms is the same.
Atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called isobars.

slides.title: Beyond Bohr: Electron Clouds
slides.kicker: The atom story is still unfolding
bullets: Even Bohr's model was not entirely correct; electrons do not follow well-defined paths like the fixed Bohr orbits.
Today we understand that electrons exist as 'electron clouds' around the nucleus.
We can predict regions where electrons are most likely to be, not exactly where they are.
slides.note: You will learn these details in higher grades!

slides.title: Journey of Atomic Models
slides.kicker: Dalton to quantum, still going
bullets: Models evolved from Dalton's indivisible particle to Thomson's positive and negative charges to Rutherford's nuclear model.
Bohr's model added energy levels, and the modern quantum mechanical atomic model followed.
As Fig. 8.16 shows, the exploration of the atom is far from over; exciting discoveries still lie ahead!
slides.note: Your journey mirrors science's — every model is a step, not the end!

flashcards.front: What is the maximum number of electrons a shell can hold?
flashcards.back: Given by the formula 2n^2, where n is the shell number: K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 18.

flashcards.front: How many electrons can the outermost shell of an atom hold?
flashcards.back: At most 8 electrons; the first shell can accommodate a maximum of two.

flashcards.front: In what order are the shells of an atom filled with electrons?
flashcards.back: Stepwise from the shell closest to the nucleus: K, L, M, N. L fills only after K is complete.

flashcards.front: What is the electronic configuration of an atom?
flashcards.back: The distribution of electrons among the various shells of the atom.

flashcards.front: How do we build up 2-D atomic structures of elements?
flashcards.back: Add one electron to the appropriate energy level each time the atomic number is increased by 1.

flashcards.front: An atom has mass number 23 and 11 protons. Who is it?
flashcards.back: Sodium, the soft metal that reacts vigorously with water, with 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons.

flashcards.front: What is the combining capacity of an element?
flashcards.back: The number of hydrogen or chlorine atoms with which one atom of the element can combine.

flashcards.front: What are the valence shell and valence electrons?
flashcards.back: The valence shell is the outermost shell containing electrons; the electrons in it are valence electrons.

flashcards.front: What is an octet, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: Eight electrons in the outermost shell. A complete octet, or 2 for helium, makes an atom stable and largely unreactive.

flashcards.front: Why is the valency of carbon 4?
flashcards.back: Carbon, 2, 4, cannot easily gain or lose its four valence electrons, so it shares four electrons to complete its octet.
Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, due to different numbers of neutrons.

flashcards.front: Name the three isotopes of hydrogen.
flashcards.back: Protium (about 99.98 percent), deuterium (about 0.015 percent) and tritium (in traces). Each has one proton.

flashcards.front: Why do isotopes have similar chemical properties?
flashcards.back: They have the same number of electrons and electronic configuration; chemical properties depend mainly on valence electrons.

flashcards.front: Which isotope dates ancient fossils and which treats cancer?
flashcards.back: C-14 dates fossils and artefacts in archaeology and geology; Co-60 is used in radiation treatment for cancer.
Atoms of different elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

flashcards.front: Which three elements with mass number 40 are isobars?
flashcards.back: Calcium (Z = 20), potassium (Z = 19) and argon (Z = 18) all have mass number 40.

flashcards.front: How does the modern model picture electrons?
flashcards.back: As electron clouds around the nucleus; we can predict likely regions, not exact paths.

quiz.q: Using the 2n^2 rule, how many electrons can the M-shell (n = 3) hold?
quiz.why: 2n^2 with n = 3 gives 2 x 3^2 = 18 electrons.

quiz.q: Hydrogen has atomic number 1. Where does its only electron sit?
quiz.why: Filling starts from the shell closest to the nucleus, the K-shell.

quiz.q: The L-shell starts filling only after which shell is complete?
quiz.why: Electrons fill stepwise K, L, M, N; L comes only after K is complete.

quiz.q: The M-shell can hold 18 electrons. Why does it stop at 8 in some atoms?
options: Because the outermost shell is capped at 8
Because electrons pair only in twos
quiz.why: The outermost shell can accommodate at most 8 electrons, whatever its 2n^2 capacity.

quiz.q: What is the distribution of electrons among the shells of an atom called?
quiz.why: The book defines electronic configuration as the distribution of electrons among shells.

quiz.q: Table 8.4 gives electron distributions for the first how many elements?
quiz.why: Table 8.4 and Fig. 8.11 cover the first eighteen elements.

quiz.q: An atom has 11 protons and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it have?
quiz.why: Neutrons = mass number - protons = 23 - 11 = 12; the atom is sodium.

quiz.q: In H2O, oxygen combines with two hydrogen atoms. What is oxygen's combining capacity?
quiz.why: Oxygen combines with two hydrogens in water, so its combining capacity is two.

quiz.q: What is the combining capacity of nitrogen in NH3 (ammonia)?
quiz.why: Nitrogen combines with three hydrogen atoms in ammonia.

quiz.q: Sodium has electronic configuration 2, 8, 1. What is its valency?
quiz.why: Sodium loses its one valence electron to complete its octet, so its valency is 1.

quiz.q: How many electrons make an octet in the outermost shell?
quiz.why: An octet means 8 electrons in the outermost shell; helium is stable with 2.

quiz.q: Carbon has configuration 2, 4. Why does it share electrons rather than gain or lose them?
options: It cannot easily gain or lose four electrons
It already has a complete octet
It has more than four valence electrons
quiz.why: With four valence electrons, carbon shares all four to complete its octet, so valency 4.

quiz.q: Isotopes of an element have the same ___ but different ___.
quiz.why: Isotopes share the atomic number but differ in neutrons, so mass numbers differ.

quiz.q: Which hydrogen isotope contains two neutrons?
quiz.why: Tritium has one proton and two neutrons; deuterium has just one neutron.

quiz.q: Which isotope is used as a fuel in nuclear reactors to generate electricity?
quiz.why: The book lists U-235 as the fuel in nuclear power plant reactors.

quiz.q: Carbon-14 has six protons. How many neutrons does it have?
quiz.why: Mass number 14 minus 6 protons gives 8 neutrons; carbon isotopes differ in neutrons.

quiz.q: Isotopes boil at different temperatures. Why are their chemical properties still similar?
options: Same electrons and same electronic configuration
quiz.why: Chemical properties depend mainly on valence electrons, which are identical in isotopes.

quiz.q: Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same ___ but different ___.
quiz.why: The book defines isobars as same mass number, different atomic numbers.

quiz.q: Argon has atomic number 18 and mass number 40. How many neutrons does it have?
quiz.why: Neutrons = mass number - protons = 40 - 18 = 22.

quiz.q: Why did scientists move beyond Bohr's idea of fixed orbits?
options: Electrons exist as clouds, not well-defined paths
quiz.why: Bohr's model was not entirely correct; electrons exist as electron clouds around the nucleus.

examples.title: Riddle of the Soft Metal
examples.problem: An atom has a mass number of 23 and 11 protons. It is a soft metal that reacts vigorously with water. Who is it and how many neutrons does it have?
steps: Atomic number equals the number of protons, so Z = 11.
The element with atomic number 11 is sodium, the soft metal that reacts vigorously with water.
Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = 23 - 11.
examples.answer: The atom is sodium, with 12 neutrons (23 - 11) and electronic configuration 2, 8, 1.

examples.title: Configuring an Oxygen Atom
examples.problem: Oxygen has atomic number 8. Write its electronic configuration and find its valency.
steps: Oxygen has 8 electrons to place, filling shells from the one closest to the nucleus outward.
The K-shell (n = 1) holds a maximum of 2 electrons, so 2 electrons go into K.
The remaining 6 electrons go into the L-shell, which can hold up to 8.
The configuration is 2, 6. Oxygen has 6 valence electrons, more than four, so it tends to gain electrons.
It gains 2 electrons to complete its octet.
examples.answer: Electronic configuration 2, 6; the valency of oxygen is 2.

examples.title: Combining Capacity from Formulas
examples.problem: Using the formulas NH3 (ammonia) and MgCl2 (magnesium chloride), find the combining capacities of nitrogen and magnesium.
steps: In ammonia, one nitrogen atom combines with three hydrogen atoms.
So the combining capacity of nitrogen is 3.
In magnesium chloride, one magnesium atom combines with two chlorine atoms.
So the combining capacity of magnesium is 2.
examples.answer: Nitrogen has combining capacity 3; magnesium has combining capacity 2.

examples.title: Counting Nucleons in Isobars
examples.problem: Potassium (Z = 19), argon (Z = 18) and calcium (Z = 20) each have mass number 40. Find the neutrons in each and explain why they are isobars.
steps: Each atom has 40 nucleons in total but a different atomic number, so they are isobars.
examples.answer: K-40 has 21 neutrons, Ar-40 has 22, Ca-40 has 20; same mass number 40 with different atomic numbers makes them isobars.
